routes.description: Establish that human sin violates God's holy law and that reconciliation coherently requires the gracious, substitutionary work of Christ rather than human moral accounting.
routes.successCriteria: The route is completed by grounding humanity's need in sin, connecting forgiveness to divine holiness and justice, and locating effective reconciliation in Christ's scripturally attested sacrifice.

motionBridge.description: Show that Christ's atonement is the coherent and scripturally grounded means by which God forgives while maintaining holiness and justice.

centralBridges.description: Establish that fallen humanity is unable to secure reconciliation through its own deeds or repentance.
Explain how substitution joins divine mercy to the vindication of God's law rather than suspending justice.
Connect Christ's priesthood and sacrifice to the Old Testament system and the wider biblical account.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish Spirit-produced obedience after salvation from deeds offered as its basis.
Account for the authority and coherence of the scriptural sources used to establish atonement.

routes.description: Establish that God coherently forgives sincere repentants directly and judges accountable deeds, while disputing the scriptural necessity and historical grounding of substitutionary atonement.
routes.successCriteria: The route is completed by grounding direct forgiveness and moral accounting in the Qur'an and biblical texts, while showing that inherited guilt and substitution are unnecessary or later doctrinal developments.

motionBridge.description: Show that repentance, divine mercy, and accountable deeds provide a coherent and scripturally grounded account of sin and salvation without substitution.

centralBridges.description: Explain why principled direct forgiveness can remain consistent with divine holiness and justice.
Ground judgment in personal conduct rather than inherited guilt or an inability requiring substitution.
Show that biblical support for substitution reflects Pauline or later development rather than the original teaching of Jesus and earlier scripture.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Preserve a material role for enabled human obedience and repentance in the account of salvation.
Explain the textual and transmission distinctions involved in appeals to the Qur'an and Bible.

sections.title: Direct forgiveness, holiness, and justice
sections.rationale: The motion centrally turns on whether forgiveness requires an objective satisfaction of divine law or can be granted directly through principled mercy.

sections.title: Human fallenness and personal responsibility
sections.rationale: Each route requires an account of the sinner's condition that determines whether accountable repentance is sufficient or supernatural liberation and representation are necessary.

sections.title: The place of deeds in salvation
sections.rationale: The competing routes must explain scriptural commands and judgments concerning deeds while identifying whether obedience is a basis, condition, or result of salvation.

sections.title: The coherence and operation of atonement
sections.rationale: The atonement route must specify how Christ's role makes forgiveness coherent, while the direct-forgiveness route disputes whether punishment or payment through an innocent substitute is intelligible.

sections.title: Scriptural continuity and doctrinal development
sections.rationale: Because the motion asks which account is scripturally grounded, each route must connect its salvation model to earlier scripture and explain the provenance of later atonement claims.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.proposition: The Qur'an teaches that sincere repentance brings God's direct forgiveness and that final judgment accounts for human deeds.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Shabir Ally immediately before this uninterrupted opening presentation.

response.rationale: This constructive directly advances the direct-forgiveness and accountable-deeds route by linking sincere repentance to forgiveness and final judgment to deeds.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: A strong motion-level constructive, though the justice principle governing forgiveness remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claims about sincere repentance, forgiveness, and final accounting are clear; conditions governing sincerity and forgiveness remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical account rests on an asserted Qur'anic teaching without developing interpretive qualifications or competing passages.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Repentance, forgiveness, and deed accounting form a coherent route, though their exact relationship is not fully explained.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Qur'an is invoked as direct support, but the excerpt supplies no specific passage or developed interpretive warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the complete con motion route and establishes its basic salvation model.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move states its own account and does not materially represent or attack a live alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly says sincere seekers receive God's forgiveness and that final reckoning concerns human deeds.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.proposition: The Old Testament supports obedience, repentance, and divine forgiveness without making blood payment or Christ's substitutionary death necessary.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Shabir Ally's uninterrupted opening presentation following his explicit introduction.

response.rationale: This constructive attacks the claimed biblical necessity of Christological atonement by appealing to Old Testament reward, punishment, repentance, and forgiveness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is relevant and substantial, but the excerpt itself acknowledges sacrifices without fully explaining their significance.

precisionFindings.rationale: The thesis is recoverable, but its broad claim about the Old Testament outruns the excerpt's treatment of the sacrificial system.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion that blood payment or substitution is unnecessary is stronger than the limited textual survey supplied.

charity.alternative: Old Testament sacrifices may provide typological or objective atonement support rather than merely accompany repentance.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move mentions Levitical sacrifices but does not engage their strongest typological or atonement-based interpretation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from available forgiveness to the nonnecessity of atonement needs a bridge excluding sacrificial or typological grounding.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Broad Old Testament claims receive limited textual support, and the acknowledged sacrifices are not adequately analyzed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks a central scriptural-witness bridge, although it does not settle the whole canon.

representationalCharity.rationale: Omitting the sacrificial system's strongest atonement interpretation materially weakens the opposed biblical-continuity case.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites pervasive deed judgment and forgiveness in the Old Testament while expressly noting Levitical animal sacrifices.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.proposition: Genesis and the poetic language of the Psalms do not establish inherited original sin, while the Old Testament assigns people responsibility for their own conduct.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Shabir Ally's uninterrupted opening presentation following his explicit introduction.

response.rationale: This constructive supports personal responsibility by denying that Genesis and poetic Psalms establish inherited guilt and by invoking individual conduct.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It establishes a clear anthropology relevant to the route, though the representative-headship alternative is not developed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is clear, but inherited guilt, original sin, and inherited fallenness are not sharply distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The Old Testament argument is plausible, but the move treats silence and poetic language as more conclusive than established.

charity.alternative: The Christian claim may concern Adamic representation or inherited fallenness rather than personal inheritance of Adam's culpable act.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move does not distinguish inherited guilt from corruption, mortality, or representative consequences.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The scriptural-silence route is intelligible, but it does not exclude representative or consequence-based accounts of the fall.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Genesis and Old Testament responsibility are relevant evidence, though the textual comparison remains selectively summarized.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central con bridge grounding judgment in personal conduct rather than inherited guilt.

representationalCharity.rationale: The conflation narrows the strongest opposing anthropology and affects the force of the rebuttal.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt denies that Genesis teaches transmitted original sin and appeals to the absence of that retrospective claim elsewhere.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.proposition: Substitutionary and victory accounts are incoherent when they portray God as punishing his innocent son, receiving payment from him, or offering him as bait for Satan.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Shabir Ally's uninterrupted opening presentation following his explicit introduction.

response.rationale: This constructive attacks the justice-mercy bridge by questioning punishment of an innocent son, payment to God, and ransom-as-bait models.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The objections are central and pointed, but several distinct atonement theories are grouped together.

precisionFindings.rationale: The payment objection is clear, but substitution, payment, ransom, and Christus Victor are treated as a loosely unified target.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Questions expose explanatory burdens but do not by themselves establish that all substitutionary or victory accounts are incoherent.

charity.alternative: A voluntary divine self-offering by the incarnate Son need not be an unwilling third party's punishment or a literal commercial transfer.
charity.decisiveQualification: The objection omits voluntariness, Trinitarian agency, and noncommercial accounts of satisfaction.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The questions identify genuine tensions, but the conclusion generalizes from particular payment and bait formulations to broader theories.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Historical formulations are asserted and rhetorically tested, with little direct textual or doctrinal substantiation in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central claim that substitution coherently joins mercy and justice.

representationalCharity.rationale: Those omissions materially weaken the strongest substitutionary account and carry much of the claimed incoherence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks to whom the penalty is paid and why God would exact it from his son, while also invoking bait imagery.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.proposition: Paul's references to judgment by deeds and James's treatment of faith and works preserve moral accounting that conflicts with justification through Christ's death.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Shabir Ally's uninterrupted opening presentation following his explicit introduction.

response.rationale: This constructive supports a development-conflict thesis by contrasting Pauline justification with judgment by deeds and James on faith and works.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The canonical tension is directly raised, but dependence and contradiction are asserted more than demonstrated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The Pauline-versus-James thesis is clear, but the scope of conflict and meaning of justification are insufficiently delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling James an obvious reply and Paul inconsistent exceeds the limited chronology and exegesis supplied.

charity.alternative: Paul and James may address different errors or senses of justification while both affirm transformed conduct and judgment.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move does not test semantic, audience, or contextual harmonization before declaring disagreement.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Relevant New Testament books are identified, yet their language, chronology, and contexts are not comparatively demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central con claim of Pauline or later doctrinal development.

representationalCharity.rationale: The omitted harmonization is a strong live alternative, so describing Paul as slipping up materially weakens representation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls James 2 an obvious reply to Galatians and Romans and alleges conflict over justification through Jesus's death.

moves.speaker: James White

moves.attributionBasis: The moderator calls James White to speak, and this passage follows his opening acknowledgments without another handoff.

components.text: Explain how direct forgiveness of sincere repentance remains consistent with God's justice and holy law.
Address the asserted role of final deed accounting in the proposed direct-forgiveness model.

response.rationale: The move supplies a contrary requirement that forgiveness preserve divine holiness, but it does not directly assess sincere repentance or deed accounting.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The contrary material sharply identifies the central justice issue, though it leaves both target components unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The ground-of-forgiveness thesis is clear and stable, though the nature of the required ground remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The link between holiness and a required objective ground is plausible but asserted rather than fully derived.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central pro bridge linking divine holiness, law, justice, and forgiveness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily states a positive requirement and does not materially reconstruct the competing account.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.proposition: Adam's representative rebellion brought spiritual death, leaving fallen people unable to do good or come to Christ apart from supernatural grace.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator calls James White to speak, and this passage continues his uninterrupted opening presentation.

Address the appeal to Old Testament personal responsibility for each person's own conduct.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive inheritance issue but leaves the opposing scriptural-responsibility component substantially untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The anthropology is recoverable, but guilt, rebellion, death, inability, and representation are not consistently distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The universal representative conclusion is asserted more strongly than the excerpt's limited textual warrant supports.

charity.decisiveQualification: The move does not distinguish inherited culpability from inherited conditions or consequences.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt narrates Adam's willful rebellion but supplies limited support for progeny-wide guilt and incapacity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central pro claim that fallen humanity cannot secure reconciliation unaided.

representationalCharity.rationale: The missing distinction blunts contact with the strongest personal-responsibility position but does not amount to gross caricature.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes Adam's informed rebellion as plunging him and his progeny into spiritual rebellion, death, and separation.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.proposition: Human enslavement to sin prevents people from coming to Christ without God's gracious drawing and liberating action.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening-statement context and first-person Christian advocacy identify James White as the speaker.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly advances the central human-need bridge with a specific text, though broader inability remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim about inability and divine drawing is clear; the exact sense and operation of drawing remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited verse supports inability to come, but equating it with comprehensive slavery requires additional exegesis.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The stated inability and need for drawing form a stable inference, with the slavery equivalence as an implicit bridge.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move strongly supports the central pro bridge concerning humanity's inability apart from grace.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops its own scriptural anthropology without materially representing an opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt quotes John 6:44 and interprets inability to come to Christ as requiring God's gracious drawing and enablement.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.proposition: Christ's substitutionary atonement permits God to extend mercy and grace without undoing justice or disregarding divine law.
moves.attributionBasis: The continuous opening statement, Christian first-person framing, and transition into the gospel identify James White securely.

response.rationale: This constructive advances substitution as the mechanism by which mercy operates without simply ignoring sin or violating divine law.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly states the core justice-mercy function, but the mechanics of substitution remain underexplained.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is clear, though how mercy transcends rather than undoes justice is left as an implicit mechanism.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asserts substitution's necessity and success without fully defending why direct principled mercy cannot preserve justice.

charity.alternative: Direct forgiveness may be principled and law-respecting without amounting to an arbitrary wink at sin.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move treats the main alternative as disregard of sin rather than engaging a principled direct-mercy model.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The route is coherent if substitution vindicates law, but that crucial mechanism is asserted rather than demonstrated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move provides a theological explanation but little textual support or defended comparison with direct forgiveness.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central pro bridge joining divine mercy, justice, and law through substitution.

representationalCharity.rationale: That weakened contrast materially helps the substitution inference, though the positive atonement claim remains independently recognizable.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts hopeless strict justice and lawless disregard with mercy and grace made possible by substitutionary atonement.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.proposition: Good deeds are produced by the Spirit as the result of complete redemption in Christ rather than contributions that earn or complete salvation.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained exposition of Titus and explicit description of Christian belief remain within James White's opening statement.

response.rationale: This constructive distinguishes Spirit-produced good deeds as the fruit of completed redemption from works that earn or complete salvation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The basis-versus-result distinction is clear and directly advances the subsidiary works bridge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly identifies believers, Spirit-produced conformity, good deeds, and the denial that those deeds earn salvation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The asserted doctrinal distinction matches the explanatory and scriptural framing supplied within the selected excerpt.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The causal distinction between redemption and its obedient fruit is explicit, consistent, and inferentially stable.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Spirit, union with Christ, and transformed conduct provide relevant warrant, though textual documentation remains compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move strongly supports the subsidiary pro bridge distinguishing salvation's basis from its fruits.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move states the pro account of deeds without materially reconstructing an opposing position.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt attributes believers' purification and zeal for good deeds to the Spirit and expressly denies that deeds earn salvation.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.proposition: God can forgive repentant sinners directly without violating holiness or justice when divine mercy is exercised on a principled rather than arbitrary basis.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Shabir's rebuttal, and the speaker explicitly addresses James's preceding arguments throughout the passage.

components.text: Answer the claim that forgiveness requires a ground preserving divine justice, holiness, and respect for law.
Address the claim that substitution uniquely permits mercy without undoing justice.

response.rationale: The move directly argues that evenhanded, nonarbitrary forgiveness can satisfy holiness and justice, thereby rejecting substitution's claimed exclusivity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both decisive claims and offers a principled alternative, though its account of justice remains relatively thin.

precisionFindings.rationale: The condition of nonarbitrary, evenhanded forgiveness is explicit, and the justice-and-holiness claim is clearly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Evenhandedness supplies a relevant principle, but it does not by itself establish that every justice demand is satisfied.

charity.alternative: The opposing account requires more than equal treatment: it claims violated law needs an objective ground or vindication.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply addresses arbitrariness but only partly addresses the distinct claim that law itself requires satisfaction.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from principled, equal mercy to compatibility with justice is coherent, though not exhaustive of competing justice theories.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A clear moral principle supports the claim, but scriptural support and deeper defense of the principle are limited.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central con bridge explaining how direct forgiveness can remain principled and just.

representationalCharity.rationale: The strongest alternative is recognized through justice and holiness, but its objective-ground requirement remains compressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly answers the justice-and-holiness objection by conditioning forgiveness on evenhanded, nonarbitrary divine treatment.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.proposition: People need not be morally perfect to be judged righteous because, under God's merciful accounting, their good can outweigh their faults.
moves.attributionBasis: This passage continues Shabir Ally's announced rebuttal and presents Islamic moral accounting against James White's anthropology.

components.text: Answer the claim that fallen people are so morally unable that they cannot be righteous or secure reconciliation through conduct.
Address the specific claim that people cannot come to Christ without divine drawing and liberation.

response.rationale: The reply contests total depravity through merciful accounting and biblical examples of righteous people, but it does not answer the drawing text.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the broader inability premise while leaving the specific scriptural drawing argument unaddressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The good-over-bad accounting thesis is clear, but righteousness, depravity, and salvific adequacy are not sharply distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Examples called righteous do not alone disprove moral inability or establish the proposed credit-balancing mechanism.

charity.alternative: Total inability need not mean every person is maximally bad or incapable of any socially or comparatively good act.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply treats depravity as though it entailed the absence of any biblical description of human righteousness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The presence of righteous people may challenge one formulation, but it does not establish that merits outweigh faults salvifically.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Qur'anic accounting and biblical righteous figures are relevant, though passages and interpretive bridges are not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central pro bridge of comprehensive human inability.

representationalCharity.rationale: This misses a standard decisive qualification and materially overstates what righteous examples refute.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes Qur'anic good and bad credits and biblical people called righteous to dispute absolute human depravity.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.proposition: Substitutionary justification is chiefly Pauline and gains support in later Gospels, making its attribution to Jesus historically questionable.
moves.attributionBasis: The same rebuttal speaker explicitly discusses James's citations, Paul's influence, Gospel chronology, and conservative scholarly dating.

components.text: Address the internal claim that substitution coherently preserves both divine mercy and justice.
Address the distinction between deeds as salvation's fruit and deeds as its basis.

response.rationale: The historical-development thesis bears on scriptural authority but does not contact the earlier moves' internal justice mechanism or works distinction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies substantial contrary historical material, but it does not answer the decisive components of the available targets.

precisionFindings.rationale: The development thesis is clear, but chiefly Pauline, later support, and attribution to Jesus require more precise scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Gospel chronology is relevant, but later composition alone does not establish doctrinal invention or nonattribution to Jesus.

charity.alternative: Later written sources may preserve earlier traditions, and Pauline emphasis need not imply Pauline invention.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move does not separate document date from tradition date or prominence from doctrinal origin.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The chronology supports a development possibility, but the inference to historical nonauthenticity needs independent transmission evidence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Pauline emphasis and relative Gospel dating are relevant, but the excerpt lacks detailed source-critical comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central con bridge alleging Pauline or later scriptural development.

representationalCharity.rationale: Those omitted distinctions materially affect the historical inference, although the chronology concern remains legitimate.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies Paul as substitutionary justification's proponent and argues that later Gospels increasingly support the doctrine.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.proposition: Divine enablement does not remove a person's obligation to work out salvation and therefore does not make human action dispensable.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains in Shabir Ally's rebuttal and explicitly answers James's interpretation of the adjacent verse in Philippians.

components.text: Answer the claim that good deeds are only fruits of completed salvation rather than material human participation.
Address whether divine enablement is compatible with meaningful human obligation and action.

response.rationale: The move accepts divine assistance but argues that enabled people remain obligated to act and cannot rely solely on substitution.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the basis-versus-fruit dispute and the role of enablement, though the meaning of work out is underargued.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between divine assistance and retained human obligation is explicit and consistently stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The command to work out salvation supports obligation, but not by itself the claim that works partly ground salvation.

charity.alternative: The opposing view affirms required obedience while treating it as evidence and fruit of salvation rather than its meritorious basis.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply slides from required action to the conclusion that one cannot rely on Christ's completed work alone.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Enablement and obligation are compatible, but obligation alone does not establish that human action grounds salvation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Philippians and broader biblical teaching are relevant, though the decisive lexical and contextual exegesis is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move strongly supports the subsidiary con bridge preserving a material role for enabled obedience.

representationalCharity.rationale: It recognizes transformation and enablement but underrepresents the opponent's basis-versus-fruit distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt concedes that God assists and wills good action while insisting that people must work out salvation themselves.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.proposition: Believers work out a salvation they already possess while God transforms them into people devoted to good deeds.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator's transition gives James White the next rebuttal, and he immediately addresses Shabir by name and Pauline theology.

components.text: Answer the inference that the command to work out salvation makes human deeds part of salvation's basis.
Explain how divine transformation and required good deeds fit a salvation already possessed.

response.rationale: The reply directly construes work out as expressing an already possessed salvation and explains deeds through God's transforming activity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive textual inference and integrates the role of good deeds into its alternative reading.

precisionFindings.rationale: Possession, working out, transformation, and good deeds are clearly distinguished and joined in a stable proposition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reading is coherent and contextually motivated, though already possessed is asserted without detailed lexical demonstration.

charity.alternative: The command may describe a salvation process in which enabled human action remains a real condition, not merely an effect.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply recognizes the command but assumes possession excludes conditional participation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between possessing salvation and expressing it through transformed conduct is internally stable and explanatory.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The immediate theological context supports the reading, but the key semantic claim receives limited direct exegesis.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly and strongly supports the pro subsidiary works bridge against the selected objection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The opponent's enabled-obligation reading remains reasonably represented, though its conditional force is not fully tested.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says believers work out something already possessed and links their good deeds to God's conforming and purifying work.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.proposition: The repeated Day of Atonement sacrifices prefigure Christ's unique effective sacrifice, which obtains eternal redemption and fulfills the Old Testament system.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator and questioner explicitly direct the question to James, whose answer continues through a clear closing thanks.

response.rationale: This constructive connects the Day of Atonement's repeated priestly sacrifice to Christ's unique effective offering and eternal redemption in Hebrews.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It makes a specific continuity argument, though the typological inference depends heavily on Hebrews's authority.

precisionFindings.rationale: The annual ritual, typological relation, unique Christ event, and claimed eternal efficacy are clearly identified.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move strongly supports the central scriptural-witness bridge and materially answers atonement-coherence objections.

representationalCharity.rationale: The live objection is not caricatured, but one decisive philosophical component remains only indirectly addressed.

moves.proposition: People begin in a naturally saved disposition and, after deliberate rejection, can return through sincere repentance, restitution, and God's direct forgiveness without another person paying for sin.
